Assoc name: Representation of: Dionysos/Bacchus;  Representation of: Maenads
description: This exquisite Attic red-figured cup, dating from circa 480-470 BC, is a masterful example of Greek pottery, excavated from Vulci. The interior features a dynamic depiction of a maenad, draped in a chiton and himation, her movements captured as she holds an empty oinochoe and a thyrsos, with her hair elegantly styled in a bun adorned with a red fillet. The exterior presents a vibrant scene with Dionysos, the god of wine, accompanied by satyrs and maenads, all engaged in a lively Dionysian revelry. Each figure is meticulously detailed, from the satyrs' animated gestures to the maenads poised with thyrsi and floral motifs, their garments bordered with fine line work. Notable elements include floral complexes around the handles featuring palmettes and tendrils, and the use of relief line contours for the intricate hairstyle and vine details. A Greek inscription inside adds a further layer of cultural richness to this artifact. The careful painted technique exemplifies the skilled artistry of Ancient Greece, capturing the mythological and ceremonial essence of the period.

Assoc name: Associated with: Silenos;  Representation of: Maenads
description: This Attic black-figured oinochoe, a pottery wine jug dating from 500-475 BCE, is a fine example of ancient Greek craftsmanship and artistic expression. It features a trefoil mouth and is adorned with a black design set against a red panel, encircled by a maeander border above and dots along the sides. The artist utilized white and purple as accessory colors to highlight the scene depicting two Seilenoi with long white tresses, moving to the right, and a Maenad retreating in the same direction while glancing back. The Maenad is elegantly portrayed with her hair looped up, wearing a fillet, a long chiton, and a striped himation, with her left hand raised, embodying the dynamic and expressive style typical of the period. In the background, the presence of a fruit-bearing tree adds depth and context to the scene. This piece, associated with the figures of Silenos and Maenads, was excavated from Fikellura grave 84, offering insight into its ceremonial or funerary use in ancient Greek society. It stands as a testament to the cultural and artistic interactions in Greece during this era.

Assoc name: Representation of: Herakles/Hercules (possibly);  Named in inscription: Herakles/Hercules
description: This Attic red-figured pottery cup fragment, dating to circa 500 BCE, represents the artistic tradition of Archaic Greece. The interior of this tondo sherd displays a red-figure decoration, likely depicting the right arm and wrist of a figure, possibly Herakles, with a drapery element suggesting it adorns the shoulder. Two letters from a painted Greek inscription are visible, part of a pre-firing red dipinto, potentially a name or kalos inscription. The exterior is elegantly glazed in black, and the piece bears a relief-contour. The sherd's cultural significance is denoted by the possible representation of Herakles, a classical deity celebrated for his strength and heroic deeds. This artifact was excavated at Naukratis, shedding light on the exchange and influence within ancient Greek settlements.

This rim sherd of a Chian Mature Animal Style pottery chalice, dating from approximately 610 to 580 BCE, exemplifies the artistry of East Greek, Archaic Greek culture. Crafted from pottery and embellished using painted and slipped techniques, it features distinct decorative elements. On the interior, a reserved band at the rim is followed by a streaky black glaze, punctuated by an elaborate rosette outlined in white with added red centers. The exterior is adorned with a band of dots between bands at the rim, descending to a painted decoration that includes the depiction of a sphinx—with the remaining wing visible—facing left. Discovered at the archaeological site of Naukratis, this artifact provides a glimpse into the ceremonial and artistic customs of ancient Greece, highlighting the significance of mythological motifs such as the sphinx in their visual culture.

Find spot: Excavated/Findspot: HMS Colossus;  Excavated/Findspot: St Mary's Island (off)
Assoc name: Representation of: Achilles;  Representation of: Polyxena
description: This artifact consists of five fragmented pieces from an Attic black-figure lekythos, dating approximately between 510 and 500 BCE. Crafted from pottery and employing both painting and incising techniques, these pieces depict a scene from classical mythology featuring the figures Achilles and Polyxena at a fountain. Additionally, three shoulder fragments display black-figure palmettes, possibly aligning with the main depiction. These fragments pertain to the Attic culture of ancient Greece, embodying the aesthetic and narrative style typical of the Greek section. They were excavated from HMS Colossus near St Mary's Island, providing rich insights into ancient Greek artistic conventions and mythological storytelling.

This Attic red-figured squat lekythos, dating approximately to 430-400 BCE, is an exquisite example of Greek pottery, depicting the classical deity Nike. Illustrated with a graceful, yet somewhat careless style, the figure of Nike is shown standing to the right in a tied Doric chiton, her hair elegantly looped up. She extends both hands towards a spiral plant emerging from the ground. The eye of Nike, rendered in profile with a visible eyelash, adds to the piece's delicate artistry. Beneath the depiction, a thin red line enhances the composition. Crafted from pottery and executed in the painted red-figure technique, this lekythos reflects the stylistic nuances of the period. It was excavated from Fikellura grave 37, providing valuable insight into ancient Greek burial practices and artistic expressions of divine figures.

This artifact is a rim and body sherd from a Chian Mature Animal Style pottery chalice, dating circa 610-580 BC, from the Archaic Greek period. Originating from East Greek culture, this pottery fragment has been crafted from pottery material with a white slip application. The interior of the sherd exhibits a reserved band at the rim with a streaky black glaze below, while the exterior displays a lotus flower outlined in added white with red centers. Notably, the fragment includes the hind leg and tail of a feline or sphinx, accentuated by a red patch, and possibly part of a second animal, like a lion, trailing the first figure. Complemented by elaborate rosettes and a pendant triangle, these are used as ornamental filler motifs. Excavated at the renowned site of Naukratis, this sherd provides a glimpse into the sophisticated decorative styles and iconography prevalent in East Greek pottery craftsmanship of the time.

Assoc name: Representation of: Dionysos/Bacchus;  Representation of: Ariadne;  Representation of: Maenads
description: This Attic black-figured kantharos, dating from 520-500 BCE, is a remarkable example of classical Greek pottery, crafted from painted and incised clay. The vessel features a distinct donkey-head attachment and is adorned with purple and white accessories, set against a backdrop of artistic motifs like the ivy-wreath encircling its top and the tongue-pattern detailed below the main designs. On one side (a), the kantharos depicts Ariadne, seated on an okladias, adorned with long hair, an ivy-wreath, and a chiton and himation spotted with purple, holding branches and raising a cantharos in one hand. Adjacent to her, an ithyphallic Satyr stands in a dynamic pose, shading his eyes. On the other side (b), Dionysos, the bearded god of wine, is portrayed riding an ithyphallic mule, wearing an ivy-wreath, and holding vine branches and a bridle. He is accompanied by Satyrs and a Maenad, the latter mirroring the attire and accessories of Ariadne. The mule's head is left in the natural color of the clay with detailed features highlighted in black, white, and purple. The inside of the mule's head is accented with a reddish-purple slip, with the kantharos part finished in black glaze. Though its precise find spot remains uncertain, this artifact was likely discovered in Athens, contributing richly to our understanding of Greek iconography and mythological depictions, particularly those associated with Dionysos and his retinue.

Assoc name: Representation of: Dionysos/Bacchus;  Representation of: Iachos (possibly)
description: This Attic red-figured bell-krater, dating to approximately 370 BCE, is a striking example of painted pottery from ancient Greece. The vessel portrays the scene of anodos, depicting a youthful deity—potentially Iakchos or Apollo—emerging from the ground within a cave setting, accompanied by a small representation of the flying Nike. To the left of this central figure sits Dionysos, identifiable by his thyrsos, amidst a lively assembly of maenads and a satyr. On the right, a maenad holds a tray laden with grapes, symbolizing fertility and festivity. The reverse features the image of three youths, contributing to the narrative depth of the piece. This krater was excavated from St Agata dei Goti, revealing its origins within the rich cultural tapestry of ancient Greece. The meticulously painted imagery encapsulates the religious and mythological iconography of the period, offering insight into the ceremonial and artistic practices of Attic culture.

This Attic pottery piece, dating from approximately 580-560 BC, is a black-figured pyxis or lekane with a lid, showcasing the quintessential black-on-red decorative technique of ancient Greek ceramics. With a high cover terminated by a truncated conical handle hollowed out at the top, the design is both functional and ornate. The handle is encircled by three swans in a preening posture, set against a field densely adorned with small leaves. Below this motif lies a frieze featuring mythical figures and animals: a large bird in flight flanked by a sphinx and a siren, each adorned with long hair and zigzag diadems, and another section portraying a siren with wings outspread between two lions, with fields rich in small leaves and rosettes. The vase itself carries two distinct friezes; one depicts a bird amidst sirens and panthers, while the other presents confronted sirens and lions. Each scene is framed by an intricate backdrop of small leaves. This pyxis was excavated in Athens, reflecting the rich mythological and artistic traditions of ancient Greece through its imagery of sirens and sphinxes.

Subjects: satyr; classical deity; allegory/personification; mythical figure/creature; tree/bush
description: This Attic red-figured chous, dating to circa 460 BC, vividly portrays a satyr adopting the guise of Heracles in the Garden of the Hesperides, a classical theme drawn from Greek mythology. The scene is skillfully painted on pottery, showcasing a lively satyr with a short bushy beard and rough hair radiating from his crown, advancing in a mock-heroic pose. He brandishes a club defensively against an intricately coiled snake that assails the wine-bearer's covered left arm, doubled as a shield using a wine-skin draped around his neck. The composition is spirited, with purple-tinged leaves of a tree, which supports three suspended oinochoai, accentuating the vividness of the scene. The snake's tongue, hair of the satyr, and markings on the snake and askos are highlighted in brown. The decoratively transitional eye type and initial sketches suggest adjustments in the satyr's posture, adding layers to the narrative. The pottery is bordered below by maeanders interrupted by red cross squares and above by an anthemion pattern, while an inverted palmette decorates the lower part of the handle. This artifact, unearthed in Capua, offers a window into the Greek artistic tradition and its connection to mythological allegory.

Subjects: marriage/wedding; procession; battle; horse/ass; warrior; classical deity
Assoc name: Representation of: Hera/Juno;  Portrait of: Zeus/Jupiter;  Representation of: Apollo (?);  Representation of: Hermes/Mercury (?)
description: This exquisite Attic black-figured hydria, dating from 520-500 BC, exemplifies the artistry of Archaic Greece. Crafted from pottery, the hydria features intricate painted and incised designs on red panels, bordered by ivy motifs and accented with white and purple details. The shoulder of the vessel captures a dynamic battle scene, depicting a quadriga in motion, driven by a warrior armed with a shield bearing a tripod design. The chaotic energy continues with a fallen soldier underfoot, defended by two warriors with similarly adorned shields. Below, the body of the vase illustrates a marriage procession, possibly representing Hera and Zeus, accompanied by a harmonious ensemble that may include Apollo and Aphrodite, underscoring the importance of divine presence in such rituals. Ahead, Hermes may lead with his characteristic petasos and caduceus. Completing the narrative, a lion and boar face off twice below, emphasizing themes of power and conflict. Found in Vulci, this hydria offers a captivating glimpse into the cultural and mythological themes revered in Greek society.

This exquisite Attic red-figured kylix, dating from approximately 480-470 BCE, is a testament to the artistry of ancient Greece. Crafted from pottery and adorned with painted scenes, the kylix features a compelling depiction of Apollo, the beardless classical deity, situated within the interior scene. Apollo, adorned with long, wavy hair and a laurel wreath, is portrayed seated on a diphros, clad in an himation around his legs, and playing a large kithara attached to his wrist with a sash decorated with ivy-leaf motifs. He extends a fluted phiale towards a half-seen, blazing altar styled as an Ionic column, symbolizing an altar of Apollo. The exterior scene captures a narrative of interaction; on one side, a woman, garbed in a long-sleeved chiton and an himation, approaches a bearded man offering an oinochoe, while a wreathed youth with a sceptre observes, all set against the backdrop of another Ionic column. On the opposing side, a continuation of this tableau shows partially preserved figures until only gestures remain, augmented by symbolic motifs such as a pair of hanging sandals and rolled tablets with a stylus. Details in purple, including tuning pegs, flames, and wreaths, accentuate the design, accompanied by a running maeander band within the interior and delicate afterthoughts like an exergue left in red. This vessel was unearthed in Chiusi, adding depth to our understanding of Attic craftsmanship and iconography associated with religious and musical themes.

This Attic black-figure lekythos, crafted between 500 and 490 BC in Greece, is an exquisite example of ancient Greek ceramic artistry. Made from pottery and executed with painted and incised techniques, the lekythos features a vivid scene depicting a deer flanked by two satyrs, a common motif reflecting the interplay between the natural and mythical worlds. The shoulder of the vessel is elegantly adorned with a series of rays, adding to its visual appeal. This artifact was uncovered in Fikellura grave 211, offering a glimpse into the burial practices and artistic preferences of the time. As part of the Greek section, this piece holds cultural significance, resonating with the aesthetics and mythological themes prevalent in Attic art.

This Attic black-figured oinochoe, dating to around 500 BCE, is a fine example of ancient Greek pottery characterized by its intricate painted and incised design. The vessel features a striking decoration in black on a red panel, with a lip ornamented by a chequer-pattern and the neck adorned with alternating palmettes and lotus-flowers, the palmettes being inverted. Below this, pomegranate buds and the use of white and purple accessories further enhance its visual appeal. The scene depicted is of a Maenad, a follower of Dionysus, elegantly seated on a bull moving to the right; she is shown with long hair, wearing a fillet and necklace, and dressed in a long-sleeved chiton patterned with purple spots while playing the crotala, or castanets. Vine-branches with grapes enrich the background, adding a touch of nature to the mythological tableau. This vessel was uncovered in Vulci, an area renowned for its rich archaeological finds, bringing to light the cross-cultural exchanges in Etruscan and Greek art.

This Attic black-figured pottery oinochoe, dating from 500 to 480 BCE, exemplifies the artistry of ancient Greece through its intricate depiction of a Dionysiac thiasos. Crafted from pottery with painted and incised techniques, the vessel features a trefoil mouth and a vivid black design set against a white panel, bordered by a network pattern with subtle purple highlights. Central to the scene is a Satyr, his hair looped up, energetically playing the double flute, with the sybenè, or flute case, draped over his left arm. Flanking him are two Maenads, emblematic figures of Dionysian myth and culture, each elegantly adorned in chitons and a fillet, and one sporting a leopard skin, or pardalis, knotted at the front. They are captured in mid-dance, glancing back at the Satyr, with one Maenad engaging percussively through crotala. This captivating scene, set amidst the natural motif of branches, reflects the rich symbolic and cultural iconography of the era. The oinochoe was unearthed in Nola, providing important context to the spread and influence of Attic pottery throughout ancient Greece.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: in field Inscription language: Greek Inscription script: Greek Inscription quoted: HE[ Inscription translation: He[rakles] Inscription note: Pre-firing glaze dipinto.
description: This rim sherd comes from an Attic White Ground pottery cup, dating from 500 to 480 BCE, a period bridging the Archaic and Classical phases of Greek art. The sherd is intricately adorned, featuring a sharply offset rim on the interior, glazed in black with the addition of a delicate white band. The exterior showcases a transition from black at the top of the rim to a vibrant painted scene below. This scene includes the tip of a spear on the left, suggesting the presence of Athena, while Herakles is prominently depicted to the right. Herakles, dressed in a lion's skin—meticulously detailed with dilute markings for fur, eyelashes, claws, and stippling—brandishes a club in his raised right hand. Further elements of the depiction include a circle around his pupil, anatomical details, and the strap of his sword belt, with the sword's hilt visible near his stomach. A leg of a tripod crosses his chest diagonally. Inscriptions in Greek, executed as a pre-firing glaze dipinto, are present in the field, and these likely reference Herakles ("He[rakles]"). This artifact, excavated from Naukratis, offers a glimpse into the rich iconography and mythological narratives prevalent in Attic pottery, exemplifying the cultural and artistic milieu of ancient Greece.

Find spot: Excavated/Findspot: Naukratis (according to G&R Department register)
description: This Attic red-figured pottery sherd, dating approximately to 500-490 BCE, represents the artistic conventions of Archaic Greek culture. This particular fragment, identified as a stem and tondo of a type A cup, notably lacks a disjunction between the bowl and stem, but features two scraped grooves on the stem above the foot-plate. The interior boasts a red-figure decoration depicting an ithyphallic figure, possibly a satyr, kneeling on its left leg and either raising or lowering an amphora. The attention to detail is evident in the use of dilute brown for markings on the figure's arms, body, and legs, and an accidental deposit of added red on the left calf. The preliminary sketchwork enhances the dimensionality of the scene. The exterior is glazed black, with the top of the inside of the stem reserved and glazed below. Discovered in Naukratis, according to the Greek and Roman Department register, this sherd offers valuable insight into the ceremonial or symbolic use of such vessels within ancient Greek society.

This body sherd is from an East Greek, Archaic Greek pottery chalice, specifically crafted in the Chian Simple Animal Style, circa 570-560 BCE. Made of pottery with a white slip, the interior features a streaky black glaze accentuated by two added white bands, demonstrating the sophisticated aesthetic techniques of the period. The exterior bears a painted decoration of a sphinx, positioned to the right, with its rump, chest, and part of the wing visible, indicating its significance in Greek mythology as a symbol of power and mystery. This artifact was unearthed at Naukratis, a prominent trading hub in ancient Egypt, underscoring the cross-cultural exchanges between Greek and Egyptian civilizations during the Archaic period.

Subjects: war; classical mythology; classical deity; mythical figure/creature
Assoc name: Representation of: Ajax;  Representation of: Hector;  Representation of: Athena/Minerva
description: This Attic red-figured stamnos, dating from circa 515-505 BCE, vividly depicts scenes from classical mythology. Crafted from pottery and adorned through the painted technique, the vessel features two dynamic scenes. On one side, the goddess Athena intervenes between the warriors Ajax and Hector, each portrayed in a combat stance with spears and shields. Ajax, identified by the inscription ΑIAΣ, is shown bearded with a helmet tilted back, clad in a chiton, cuirass, and greaves. Hector, whose name is inscribed in retrograde as 'Έκτωρ, bears a shield emblazoned with a Pegasos silhouette, although his face is missing. Athena, depicted with a raised arm in a gesture of prohibition, is dressed in a long chiton and mantle, her name inscribed as Ά]θήναα. The painter, Smikros, has also inscribed his signature on the vessel. On the reverse, a combat scene unfolds over a fallen warrior, with warriors identified as Ευρ[ύ]μαχ[ο]ς and others. The stamnos is further embellished with purple inscriptions and decorative bands of palmettes, key patterns, tongues, and rays. Excavated from Todi, this piece is a remarkable representation of Greek artistry and mythology.

This Attic black-figure oinochoe, dating from 480-470 BC, exemplifies the exquisite artistry of ancient Greek pottery. Crafted from pottery and employing both painted and incised techniques, the vessel features a trefoil mouth and presents a vibrant depiction of a draped maenad moving to the right, glancing back at a bearded nude satyr. This interaction between mythical figures, a hallmark of Dionysian imagery, underscores the cultural and symbolic narratives prevalent in ancient Greece. Despite a missing rim fragment, the oinochoe remains a remarkable testament to Attic craftsmanship. It was excavated from Fikellura grave 61, shedding light on the burial practices and the artistic legacy of the region during this period.

This upper body sherd originates from a Chian black-figured Sphinx and Lion Style pottery dinos, dating approximately between 610 and 580 BCE. As an exquisite example of East Greek, particularly Archaic Greek pottery, it is crafted from pottery material and demonstrates intricate painted, slipped, and incised craftsmanship. The exterior of this sherd features a decorative frieze with sphinxes facing left. Notably, the tail of the first sphinx is discernible, while a seated sphinx is depicted despite missing its top and forelegs. The detailed artistry includes added red on the hair, wing, underbelly, and haunches, with incised rosettes and pendant rosettes having red centers serving as filler ornamentation. Additional bands cap an incised pendant rosette with a red center located in the lower frieze. This piece was unearthed from the site of Naukratis, shedding light on the shared cultural and artistic dynamics between Greece and the ancient communities of North Africa.

This neck sherd originates from an Attic black-figured pottery amphora, crafted around 600 BC, during the Archaic Greek period. The fragment features a distinct black-figure decoration, portraying what might be a sphinx or siren, with only the curl of the wing and a portion of the head—adorned with added red pigment and a red fillet—still visible. Above the depiction, two black bands provide a striking contrast, while a blob rosette filled with red serves as an ornamental element in the composition. The pottery is made from traditional clay and exhibits techniques of painting and incision, typical of the era's ceramic craftsmanship. This artifact was unearthed in Naukratis, a significant trading hub in ancient Greece that facilitated cultural exchanges between Greek and Egyptian civilizations, thus providing a rich context for this piece.

This Attic Classical Greek pottery kylix, dating from 490 to 460 BCE, is a remarkable example of black-figure technique, both painted and incised. The interior depicts a draped maenad holding a circlet, while the exterior features dynamic scenes involving draped figures—some moving to the right, others riding donkeys, and on the left, a satyr harasses another draped figure. This intricate imagery, characteristic of classical mythology, brings to life the interactions between humans and mythical creatures. Crafted from pottery, this kylix exemplifies the artistic sophistication of the period despite a rim fragment being absent. The vessel was unearthed from grave 254 at Fikellura, offering a fascinating glimpse into ancient Greek funerary practices and the culture's rich mythological tapestry.

Assoc name: Representation of: Herakles/Hercules (?);  Representation of: Cretan Bull (?);  Representation of: Theseus (?);  Representation of: Bull of Marathon (?)
description: This Attic oinochoe, dating from 500 to 480 BCE, is a striking example of black-figure pottery featuring a trefoil mouth. Despite its rather worn and coarse style, the design remains captivating, with black figures set against a red panel, adorned with a border of dots above and highlighted with white accessories. The scene depicts a dramatic moment from Greek mythology: a nude, beardless male figure struggling to subdue a bull, potentially representing the legendary Heracles with the Cretan bull or Theseus with the Bull of Marathon. The bull is depicted having fallen forward onto its head and forelegs, while in the surrounding field, branches hang with items such as a chlamys, club, bow, and quiver, adding depth to the narrative. Crafted using painted and incised techniques, this vessel was excavated from Fikellura grave 95, providing a glimpse into ancient Greek burial practices and mythological symbolism.

This Attic silhouette style pottery sherd, originating from the Archaic Greek period between 510-480 BCE, possibly hails from a type A cup. It was produced using a painted technique on pottery material. The interior features a small reserved tondo adorned with a dynamic whirligig design of four frontal half-satyrs, depicted in silhouette style, forming a circle. Two satyrs raise their right hands, while the others stand with both hands on hips and elbows akimbo. The exterior of the cup is glazed in black, enhanced by a red band on the fillet at the top of the stem; the upper part of the interior of the stem is reserved, transitioning to black lower down. This artifact was unearthed in Naukratis, providing valuable insights into the trade connections and cultural interactions of ancient Greece.

description: This exquisite Attic pottery artifact is a red-figured skyphos, crafted around 510 BC. Featuring intricate paintings, side (a) depicts the god Dionysos, bearded and crowned with ivy, adorned in a long chiton with sleeves and a himation. He strides to the right, looking back, holding a cantharos and a vine with leaves and grapes, pursued by a partially obscured satyr and an ithyphallic ass. Side (b) showcases a bearded satyr, also wreathed with ivy and holding a thyrsos in each hand, amidst two ithyphallic, braying asses. The artistry is noted for its spirited drawing, small extremities, and mannered drapery, with purple used for inscriptions, wreaths, and vine leaves, and a separate brown body color for grapes. Greek inscriptions reveal the makers: Epiktetos as the painter and Pistoxenos as the creator, although part of the latter inscription is incomplete. This vibrant piece, capturing scenes rich with classical deities and symbolic animals, was likely excavated in Capua, Italy, and is a vivid representation of the cultural and mythological tapestry of ancient Greece.

This Attic red-figured hydria, dating circa 430 BC, presents a captivating scene featuring Eros and a fawn. The depiction shows Eros, characterized by short hair and a fillet with a point over his forehead, gracefully leaning with his left elbow on a raised knee while gently stroking a fawn that rests with folded legs on a rise of ground. In his left hand, Eros holds three sprigs or flowers. The artist's skill is evident, though certain elements display a transition towards a more casual execution. The use of purple adorns the fillet, sprigs, and ground lines, while brown marks are used for inner details, and the fawn's eye is rendered in a simple profile. Below the main imagery, a decorative strip features sets of three meanders interrupted by chequer squares, with the design extending to the shoulder of the vase. This vessel demonstrates the artistry and thematic preferences of the Greek cultural milieu, specifically from the Attic region. It was excavated in Nola, providing a glimpse into the dissemination and reception of Greek pottery beyond its origins.

ΠΥΘΟΔΗΛΟΣΝΡΧΕΝ, Πνθόδηλος (η)ρχεν. Inscription translation: One of the prizes from Athens
(When) Pythodelos was archon Inscription note: Inscribed 'kionedon' (letters horizontal cf. vertical, but still down the column). Pythodelos was archon 336 B.C. For the use of ηρχεν cf. Evaiveτos ηρχεν, on the Lysicrates monument, C.I.Gr. 221.
description: This Classical Greek Panathenaic amphora, crafted between 336-335 BCE during the archonship of Pythodelos, is a remarkable piece of pottery featuring painted and incised decoration in black on a red ground with white accessories. The obverse displays an archaistic depiction of Athena standing in regal demeanor between two Ionic columns, her right arm brandishing a spear and a shield on her left, adorned with traditional elements such as a high-crested helmet, aegis, and ornate chiton. The columns feature intricate scenes, with the left depicting Triptolemos in a winged chariot drawn by snakes, and the right showcasing Nike holding a staff reminiscent of those used for trophies, each accompanied by Greek inscriptions reading "One of the prizes from Athens" and marking Pythodelos's archonship. The neck of the amphora is adorned with a double honeysuckle and elongated tongue pattern. On the reverse, the amphora captures the vigorous movement of a foot-race involving four armed, beardless warriors, each in helmets and equipped with distinctive shields. This amphora, excavated from the historic site of Caere, not only illustrates the artistic excellence of the period but also commemorates the athletic events and religious significance of the Panathenaic festival, with Athena in her role as a patron deity.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription
description: This Attic red-figured cup from circa 520-500 BC exemplifies the ceramic artistry of ancient Greece. Crafted from pottery and skillfully painted, the cup's interior highlights a vivid scene within a thin red circle, depicting a wreathed ithyphallic satyr kneeling to the right on a cushion. The satyr holds a large open bowl on his knees, with both hands resting inside it. Surrounding the satyr, the Greek inscription "ΗΟΠΑΙΣ ΚΑΛΟΣ" translates to "the boy is beautiful," rendered in purple, which also colors the satyr's wreath. The figure features an archaic-style eye, characterized by an eyeball depicted as a dotted circle. This piece stands as a testament to the erotic and mythological themes prevalent in Greek pottery, offering insights into the cultural and social expressions of the time. The cup was excavated at Vulci, linking it to a significant archaeological site known for its wealth of Greek artifacts.

This carved cylinder seal, dating from the Early Dynastic III to the Akkadian period (2400-2200 BCE), is a striking artifact of Mesopotamian culture. Fashioned from blue-grey limestone or marble, the seal features an intricate depiction of a crossed lion and bull-man, alongside a stag and lion, highlighting the rich iconography of mythical creatures and mammalian symbols prevalent in ancient Mesopotamian art. The absence of inscriptions does not detract from the artifact's detailed craftsmanship, illustrating both its artistic and utilitarian purposes in ancient societal rituals or administrative activities. Excavated from the South East Palace in Nimrud, Iraq, this piece provides a window into the sophisticated culture and mythological tapestry of the time, serving as a testament to the skill and symbolism of ancient craftsmen in the cradle of civilisation.

This imposing artifact is a torso carved from black diorite, dating from 2150 to 2000 BC and attributed to the Third Dynasty of Ur. The polished surfaces highlight the craftsmanship, with the figure's hands clasped over its chest, clad in an embroidered tunic featuring a decorated hem visible both on the front and reverse. Though the head and lower body are missing, and the left shoulder bears damage, the statue's meticulous detailing offers insight into the artistic expression of the Mesopotamian era. This votive statue, discovered in Iraq, reflects the religious and cultural significance of material offerings during this period in ancient Mesopotamian society.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: beneath lion Inscription language: Assyrian Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription translation: .......one eighth....... Inscription note: Shows that the weight belongs in the 'heavy' mina series.
description: This Neo-Assyrian limestone measuring-weight, dating from 800 to 600 BC, is skillfully crafted in the shape of a duck. An exquisite engraving of a lion adorns the flank of the duck, signifying the weight as royal property, a typical practice in the period to denote ownership by the ruling class. Beneath the lion, a cuneiform inscription in Assyrian script indicates its classification in the "heavy" mina series, with a translation suggesting a reference to "one eighth," which may pertain to its weight measurement. This artifact, a testament to the advanced metrological practices of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, was excavated at Nimrud in present-day Iraq, providing valuable insights into the era's economic and administrative systems.

Find spot: Excavated/Findspot: Temple of Ishtar Sharrat Niphi
description: This Neo-Assyrian artifact, dated to 875-850 BCE, is a marble furniture finial or chariot fitting intricately carved in the shape of a griffin's head. The piece exhibits a large, prominent beak, a crest atop its head, and ears, highlighting the artistry of the period. Made from a smooth white stone, the griffin's eye sockets retain extensive remains of bitumen, a detail that suggests inlay work used for added depth and realism. The base of the finial features a circular dowel hole, measuring 1.8 cm in diameter and 3.5 cm deep, while two additional holes in the neck indicate where the piece would have been secured with nails to a likely wooden shaft. Excavated from the Temple of Ishtar at Sharrat Niphi in Iraq, this artifact offers insight into the ceremonial or practical uses of chariot fittings in Neo-Assyrian culture and their symbolic significance within this ancient civilization.

This Neo-Assyrian gypsum wall panel relief, crafted between 700 and 692 BCE, exquisitely depicts horses and grooms departing from the palace of the renowned Assyrian king Sennacherib. As one of three joining sections, it illustrates the sophisticated carving techniques employed by artisans of the time. The panel, carved in gypsum, offers a glimpse into the grandeur of Sennacherib's reign and the significance of equestrian imagery in Assyrian culture. Excavated from the South West Palace in Nineveh, now modern-day Iraq, this relief is a testament to the rich artistic heritage of ancient Mesopotamia.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription note: Incomplete spell listing the names of Lamashtu.
description: This Neo-Assyrian or Late Babylonian stone amulet, produced between 800-550 BCE, is a mottled green artifact designed for spiritual or protective purposes. It is notably inscribed with an incomplete spell listing the names of Lamashtu, the fearsome Mesopotamian demoness associated with ill health and misfortune. The amulet is equipped with a suspension lug, indicating it was likely worn or carried as a talisman. The reverse side is intricately engraved with a figure of Lamashtu, underscoring its role as a protective object against evil forces. Engraved with care, this artifact testifies to the rich tradition of warding off demonic influences in ancient Mesopotamian culture. It was found in southern Iraq, contributing vital insights into regional practices of demonology and personal protection during the period.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: Akkadian Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription note: States that it was presented by Sennacherib to his son Esarhaddon.
Assoc name: Named in inscription: Sennacherib;  Named in inscription: Esarhaddon
description: This Neo-Assyrian limestone artifact, circa 882 BCE, is a meticulously carved lion's head originally crafted with inlaid features, though the recessed eye-sockets, wrinkled nose, and whiskers retain no traces of their former embellishments. The piece bears a cuneiform inscription in Akkadian, which reveals its significance as a gift from King Sennacherib to his son, Esarhaddon. This symbolic gesture likely held deep political or cultural significance, reflecting the era's intricate dynastic relationships within the Assyrian Empire. Unearthed from the Shamash Temple in present-day Iraq, this sculpture offers a glimpse into the artistic and ceremonial practices of the time, capturing the enduring legacy of Neo-Assyrian artistic craftsmanship and royal patronage.

This artifact is a flat, rectangular stamp-seal crafted from black steatite, dating from approximately 2000 to 1000 BCE, during the Isin-Larsa, Old Babylonian, and Kassite periods. Integral to Mesopotamian culture, the seal features a distinctive lug or boss handle on the back, permitting suspension, with a hole cleverly pierced through the handle. The base is intricately engraved with a design that includes a crescent, a bird in a rampant position, a scorpion, and a long-necked bird, embodying prevalent themes such as arachnids, birds, and celestial symbols like the sun and moon. Although the surface shows signs of abrasion, these engravings reflect the artistic expression and symbolism of ancient Mesopotamian society. This seal was excavated at Diqdiqqah, near Ur in present-day Iraq, offering glimpses into the utilitarian and ceremonial functions of such objects within the cultural tapestry of the region.

This Akkadian calcite stela, dating from around 2250 BCE, depicts a female figure intricately carved in low relief. The figure is adorned with a multiple string necklace or choker, featuring a vertical division towards the back that may indicate a single plait of hair crossing it or more likely, the clasp. Below the choker hangs another looser neck ornament, the end of which rests on the right breast, while damage around the left breast suggests it was originally covered, potentially by the figure's hand. Notably, the lower lip is characterized by natural pink veining in the calcite rather than painted pigment. This fragmentary stela, unearthed at Abu Shahrain (ancient Eridu) in Iraq, provides valuable insights into the representation of women and jewelry in the Akkadian culture, underscoring themes of femininity and adornment.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription note: States that the statue was dedicated to the sun god Shamash, on behalf of Ikun-Shamash, king of Mari, by Arra'il, one of his officials.
Assoc name: Named in inscription: Shamash;  Named in inscription: Iku-Shamash;  Named in inscription: Arra'Il
description: This Early Dynastic III limestone statue, carved circa 2500 BC, represents a beardless seated man, though its head is now missing. Crafted using intricate carving techniques, the statue bears a cuneiform inscription that reveals its devotional nature. It was dedicated to the sun god Shamash by Arra'il, an official acting on behalf of Ikun-Shamash, the king of Mari. Such inscriptions provide valuable insights into the religious practices and hierarchical society of ancient Mesopotamia. The statue was excavated in Abu Habba, ancient Sippar, in modern-day Iraq, a site rich with historical significance as a center of worship and scholarship in Mesopotamian culture.

This artifact is a Halaf culture stamp-seal dating from 6000 to 5000 BC, uncovered at the archaeological site of Arpachiyah in present-day Iraq. Crafted from green steatite or serpentine, this conical or circular seal features incised geometric cross-hatched designs on its flat face, though it is partially broken. Such seals have significant historical importance, often serving administrative purposes or indicating ownership, reflecting the societal complexity and artistry of the Halaf period in Mesopotamia. The piece provides valuable insight into early computational methods and emblematic practices in ancient Mesopotamian civilization.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: Akkadian Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription note: On both sides
Assoc name: Associated with: Adad-nirari III;  Associated with: Nergal-eresh
description: This fragment of an inscribed stone stela, originating from the Neo-Assyrian period between 810-783 BCE, was unearthed in Nineveh, Iraq. It features a horizontal incised cuneiform inscription in Akkadian on both sides, documenting a royal grant by King Adad-nirari III, designating Nergal-eresh as governor of the province of Hindanu. The stela is adorned with an incised snake design along its edge, a distinctive feature amidst its heavily burnt surfaces, suggesting the effects of fire in antiquity. Crafted from stone using incised techniques, the artifact not only embodies significant historical governance practices but also reflects the symbolic importance of reptiles within Assyrian iconography. This piece provides a rare glimpse into the administrative practices of the ancient Mesopotamian empire.

Inscription:
Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: top of panel Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription note: Reverse of relief carved with so called 'standard inscription' summarising the achievements of the king, which was written across virtually every panel of the North West palace in Nimrud.
Another version of this text was written on the reverse side of the panels, invisible against the mud-brick wall.
Subjects: king/queen; flower; arms/armour; attendant; charioteer/chariot; horse/ass; cattle; wild cat/big cat; mesopotamian myth/legend
description: This Neo-Assyrian gypsum wall panel relief, dating from 874 BCE or slightly later, vividly depicts King Ashurnasirpal II on a campaign. The king is shown in a royal chariot, traversing a hilly landscape with attendants, as indicated by the schematic representation of a river and the textured ground. Ashurnasirpal II is distinguished by his conical crown and impressive beard; he brandishes two upright arrows and a lowered bow, symbolizing victory. His regalia includes a sword with a lion-decorated sheath, two rosette-adorned wristlets, and a chariot equipped with decorated quivers and a spiked shield featuring a lion's head boss. An attendant shields the king with a sunshade, while a charioteer skillfully manages the horses, highlighted by a four-rein setup, typical of Assyrian royal chariots of the era. Though only three horses are shown, such chariots likely employed a team of four, led by an armed groom who mirrors the king's wristlet ornamentation. This panel, originally part of a corner section in the North West Palace, was divided for transport in the 19th century, and features the 'standard inscription' in cuneiform at its top, echoing the king's accomplishments across the palace's panels in Nimrud. It was excavated from the North West Palace in Iraq, attesting to the rich cultural heritage of the Mesopotamian region.

description: This Middle Babylonian commemorative stone stela, dating from the 9th to the 8th century BCE, is crafted from diorite and takes the form of a boundary-stone, known as a kudurru. The artifact features a fiat panel with figures and symbols in low relief, while the majority of the cuneiform inscription resides on the flat surface, with the concluding seven lines extending lower on the stone. The stela honors Adad-etir, a dagger-bearer of Marduk, and was erected by his eldest son, Marduk-balassu-iqbi. The imagery includes a winged solar disc, a crescent, and a lion-headed mace upon a pedestal, symbolically protecting the stone and its inscriptions, the latter of which invoke dire imprecations against those who would deface it. The text also calls blessings for those who preserve it. The stela's historical context is enriched by the presence of figures like Sin, Shamash, Nergal, and Nabu, gods of ancient Mesopotamia. It was excavated from the Marduk Temple in Babylon, adding to its cultural and devotional significance.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription note: States that this statue was dedicated to the goddess Nin-shubur of the city of Der by Enzi and his son Amar-kiku.
Assoc name: Named in inscription: Nin-Shubur;  Named in inscription: Enzi;  Named in inscription: Amar-Kiku
description: This gypsum statue, originating from the Early Dynastic III period around 2400 BCE, exemplifies Mesopotamian craftsmanship with its intricate carving and an inscription on the back. Though the head is missing, the statue's polished concave underside suggests it was skillfully shaped. The cuneiform inscription reveals its dedication to the goddess Nin-Shubur of the city of Der by Enzi and his son Amar-Kiku, indicating the statue's religious and cultural significance during its time. Excavated in Iraq, this artifact provides a tangible link to the religious practices and societal hierarchies of ancient Mesopotamia.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription translation: Enannatum.
Assoc name: Named in inscription & portrayed: Enannatum I (?)
description: This Early Dynastic III stone plaque, dated to around 2450 BCE, originates from the region of Lagash, present-day Iraq, and portrays Enannatum I, an influential king or governor. The carved stone artifact depicts Enannatum in an attitude of worship, distinguished by his folded hands. Cuneiform inscriptions on the plaque further identify the figure as Enannatum. As a representative example of Mesopotamian artistry, the plaque offers insight into the religious and political landscape of ancient Lagash. Excavated at Tello, this artifact is an important piece of Mesopotamian heritage, reflecting both the craftsmanship and the cultural narratives of the period.

This exquisite Neo-Assyrian gypsum wall panel relief, dating from 700BC to 692BC, captures a vivid scene from the ancient world, depicting horses and grooms departing from the palace of the renowned king Sennacherib. Carved with careful attention to detail, the relief is one of three joining slabs that together narrate a story of regal movement and ceremonial procession. As a product of the South West Palace in Nineveh, the piece exemplifies the artistic prowess and cultural expressions prevalent in Mesopotamia during this period. Excavated from its original context in modern-day Iraq, it offers a glimpse into the grandeur and complexity of Assyrian royal life, reflecting the significance of horses and grooms within the societal hierarchy and ceremonial practices of the era.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription note: Dedication to goddess Nanshe, on behalf of Nam-Mahani, by lady Ninkagina, daughter of Kaku.
Assoc name: Named in inscription: Nanshe;  Named in inscription: Nammahani;  Named in inscription: Kaku
description: This exquisite statuette from the Third Dynasty of Ur, dating back to 2113-2111 BCE, elegantly merges animal form with human likeness through its depiction of a reclining human-headed bull. Skillfully carved from black stone with polished surfaces, it is adorned with a cuneiform inscription that bears a dedication to the Mesopotamian goddess Nanshe. This inscription denotes an offering made by Lady Ninkagina, daughter of Kaku, on behalf of Nam-Mahani, suggesting a strong cultural and religious undertone. The artifact, embodying the artistic and devotional practices of early Mesopotamian civilization, was excavated from the historic site of Lagash in present-day Iraq, contributing to our understanding of the religious and societal dynamics of the era.

This Jemdet Nasr period white stone stamp-seal, dating from 3000 to 2900 BC, is intricately carved in the form of a couchant boar. The artifact is meticulously crafted using piercing and drilling techniques, featuring a design on its base depicting one animal in pursuit of another. Despite chipping and cracks on the front, the seal's vivid imagery captures the artistic endeavours of early Mesopotamian civilization. Characterized by a laterally pierced hole, the seal was excavated from the historic city of Ur, nestled in present-day Iraq, shedding light on the symbolic and functional role of seals in ancient Sumerian society.

This Early Dynastic III stone tumbler, dating to approximately 2500 BC, is a remarkable artifact from ancient Mesopotamia. Carved from green travertine, this piece is distinguished by its tall cylindrical shape and the presence of striking horizontal reddish veins. Expertly polished, the tumbler exemplifies the sophisticated stone-carving techniques of the period. The artifact was excavated from the Royal Cemetery at Ur, underlining its significance within the context of ancient Mesopotamian funerary practices and the opulence associated with royal burials. This finely crafted piece provides valuable insight into the material culture and artistry of one of history's earliest civilizations.

This exquisite Akkadian shell lamp, dating from 2300 to 2100 BCE, is a testament to the craftsmanship of Mesopotamian culture. Fashioned from shell, the lamp features a prominently engraved bird's head at the upper end of its aperture, symbolizing the artistic naturalism prevalent in ancient Akkadian society. Its decoration is further enhanced by meticulously incised wavy lines, showcasing the intricate technique employed by its creators. This artifact was unearthed at the Royal Cemetery of Ur in present-day Iraq, a site renowned for its rich historical significance and ties to the illustrious Sumerian and Akkadian civilizations.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: FRONT Inscription language: Babylonian Inscription transliteration: ir-ra saga. Inscription translation: Irra, priest.
Subjects: mammal; mythical figure/creature; sun/moon; deity; leaf; arms/armour; vessel; devotee/worshipper; planet/constellation
description: This Akkadian cylinder seal, dating from 2400-2200 BCE, is meticulously carved from greenstone. The seal's intricate design features an array of figures and scenes: a worshipper in a fringed robe stands with clasped hands beneath a recut star and crescent, symbolizing celestial bodies. A bearded god, donning a striped skirt, holds a mace and a possible whip over his right shoulder while managing the halter of a mythical bird-lion. Another scene depicts a bearded deity, clad in a loin-cloth, kneeling to pierce a bull's neck. Above the bull, a figure in a striped skirt extends both hands amidst streaming water, with foliage depicted near the figure's left hand. The terminal illustration shows a pot releasing a vertical stream of water, echoing the theme of abundance or purification. An unframed line of Babylonian inscription reads "Irra, priest," offering insight into the seal's significance or ownership. This artifact, excavated from the South East Palace in Nimrud, Iraq, serves as a testament to the symbolic and religious intricacies of Akkadian culture.

This conical stamp-seal, originating from the Halaf culture between 6000 and 5000 BCE, is a notable piece of early Mesopotamian craftsmanship. Made from limestone and featuring a faint blue glaze, the seal's geometric design comprises criss-cross incised lines on its flat circular base. The artifact is distinguished by a high pierced lug at the back, showcasing intricate incising and perforation techniques. As a representative of Halaf artistry, this stamp-seal exemplifies the era's aesthetic and functional utility, likely serving as a tool for pressing patterns onto a soft material, such as clay or dough. Excavated from Arpachiyah in modern-day Iraq, it provides valuable insight into the social and cultural practices of early Mesopotamian societies.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: shoulder Inscription language: Akkadian Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription translation: Urlammarak viceroy of AN.PA.x Inscription note: Additional cuneiform doodling on the back.
Culture: Early Dynastic II; Early Dynastic III
description: This captivating Early Dynastic II-III calcite statue, dating back to around 2600 BCE, originates from Mesopotamia and was found in Iraq. The statue depicts a bearded man with long hair, skillfully carved and polished from calcite. Notably, the nose appears to have been a separate attachment, suggesting advanced crafting techniques of the period. The statue is adorned with an Akkadian cuneiform inscription, which is positioned on the shoulder, reading "Urlammarak viceroy of AN.PA.x." Additional cuneiform doodling adorns the back, offering a glimpse into the textual practices of the time. This artifact serves as an artistic representation of early Mesopotamian sculpture, providing insight into the cultural and leadership structures of the era.

This Old Babylonian limestone basin, dating to approximately 1800 BCE, is an exquisite example of Mesopotamian artistry. The exterior of the basin is adorned with intricately carved low-relief scenes depicting a warrior engaged in combat with a lion, a powerful motif symbolizing strength and heroism. Notably, the central portion of the base of the basin is worn through, suggesting it may have been used as a socket. Crafted with precision, this carved piece highlights the artistic techniques and cultural narratives of the era. The basin was excavated in the historic region of Nineveh, present-day Iraq, offering a glimpse into the rich cultural heritage of ancient Mesopotamia.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: bottom of panel Inscription script: cuneiform Inscription note: Traces of the standard inscription.
Subjects: jewellery; vessel; musician; musical instrument; king/queen; prince/princess (?); eunuch; attendant; cattle; charioteer/chariot; food/drink; arms/armour; mesopotamian myth/legend
Assoc name: Representation of: Ashurnasirpal II;  Representation of: Shalmaneser III
description: This Neo-Assyrian gypsum wall panel, crafted between 875-860 BCE, vividly depicts a royal bull hunt in relief, highlighting the prowess of King Ashurnasirpal II. The scene captures the royal chariot, rushing to the right, over a fallen bull, with the king himself, in his distinctive royal hat, turning to confront another bull charging from behind. In a display of might, he grasps the bull by its horn while driving his sword into its neck, later resting his bow to pour a triumphant libation of wine. The panel is animated with royal bodyguards, all beardless eunuchs, wielding maces, and attendants carrying a fan and sunshade, while an officer, likely the future King Shalmaneser III, is depicted facing Ashurnasirpal, adorned in similar attire. A chief eunuch stands alongside, and musicians with harps perform to the right of the scene. Behind the king, an armed horseman, bearing a shield, leads a royal steed with a saddlecloth in a geometric pattern, reminiscent of Middle Eastern designs still seen today. The lower edge of the panel bears traces of cuneiform inscriptions, adding to the historical richness of the artifact. Excavated from the North West Palace in Iraq, this artwork exemplifies the grandeur of Assyrian royal iconography and storytelling.

This ancient chlorite cylinder seal, originating from the Third Dynasty of Ur and dated between 2100-2000 BCE, exemplifies Mesopotamian craftsmanship with its standard presentation scene. The seal features a shaven-headed worshipper, clad in a fringed robe, who is depicted raising his right hand as he is led by a hand-holding goddess. This goddess, adorned in a striped robe with a double-rolled hem and a single pair of horns on her head-dress, approaches another seated goddess with a similar head-dress and a flounced robe, though the flounces have faded over time. The seated deity, extending her right hand, is positioned beneath a faint crescent moon, enhancing the celestial theme. The original scene, now heavily worn and recut, has been altered by a new, framed three-line inscription that has obliterated the worshipper, leaving the surface considerably flatter on one side. The seal was excavated in the historic city of Ur, providing valuable insights into the religious and cultural practices of the era.

This incised chert artifact, originating from the Halaf culture between 6000 and 5000 BC, is a sickle-shaped stamp-seal or amulet with a serrated edge, serving both decorative and possibly functional purposes. Its design includes a pierced lobe for suspension, suggesting it may have been worn or displayed. Despite its age, it remains substantially intact, though with noted chipping and deposit accumulation. As an example of early Mesopotamian craftsmanship, this piece offers valuable insights into the symbolic and utilitarian aspects of objects from the era. It was excavated at Arpachiyah, a site in modern-day Iraq, further enriching our understanding of ancient Halafian society and its use of stamped imagery.

This sub-circular stamp-seal, crafted from serpentine and dating between 6000-5000 BC, originates from the Halaf culture of ancient Mesopotamia. The seal is intricately incised with a geometric design featuring a central cross motif surrounded by smaller incisions, indicative of its meticulous craftsmanship. It is pierced for suspension, suggesting it may have also served as an amulet. Despite being chipped and abraded, the seal remains a valuable artifact, offering insights into the symbolic and decorative practices of the Halaf people. This piece was excavated at Arpachiyah in present-day Iraq, reflecting the rich cultural heritage of the region during the Neolithic period.

This short cylinder seal, originating from the Jemdet Nasr period in Mesopotamia, dates back to circa 3000-2900 BCE. Expertly carved and engraved from dark yellowish stone, it features a shallow relief depicting a temple alongside a quadruped walking to the right, emblematic of the era's artistic and cultural motifs. This seal offers insight into the symbolism and practices of the time, possibly relating to religious or administrative activities. Discovered in southern Iraq, this artifact underscores the region's rich archaeological heritage and its role in early urban development in the ancient Near East.

This artifact is a sherd, specifically the base of a vessel, originating from the Tang dynasty in China, crafted between 618-906 CE. Made from white glazed porcelain, it features a low bi footring, a notable characteristic of Tang ceramic wares. The glaze within the footring displays numerous inclusions, indicative of the vessel's artisanal production techniques. This piece encapsulates the advanced ceramic craftsmanship of the Tang period, reflecting the era's aesthetic values and functional designs in pottery. It was excavated from Dar al-Khilafa, offering valuable insights into the trade and distribution of Chinese porcelain during this culturally rich period in Chinese history.

This artifact is a sherd from a lid dating back to the Tang dynasty, produced between 618-906 CE, originating from China. Crafted from white glazed porcelain with a subtle greenish tinge, the piece exhibits intricate cut patterns, suggesting its use as part of an incense burner or potpourri container. Both sides of the sherd are glazed, showcasing the refined ceramic techniques of the period. This exquisite piece was unearthed at Dar al-Khilafa, offering a glimpse into the sophistication and utility of Tang dynasty porcelain artifacts.

This neck-less jar from the Tang dynasty, dating between 618-906 CE, exemplifies the intricacy of marbled ware pottery. Crafted from red and buff earthenware stoneware, the jar showcases a striking marbled effect achieved by mixing clays of different colors prior to shaping. A transparent yellow lead glaze covers the piece, highlighting the marbled design and enhancing its aesthetic appeal. This artifact, a testament to the innovative ceramic techniques of the Tang dynasty, was discovered in China, underscoring the region's rich cultural heritage in pottery craftsmanship.

This figure, originating from the Tang dynasty between 618-906 CE, exemplifies the artistic and cultural expressions of this period. Crafted from pigmented and gilded earthenware, the piece is a representation of a lokapala, a guardian deity, highlighting the blend of spiritual significance and ornamental sophistication prevalent in Tang art. The use of gold suggests a high level of craftsmanship and the importance placed on such figures in the religious or ceremonial contexts of the era. Discovered in China, this artifact embodies the remarkable artistic traditions of the Tang dynasty, providing insights into the period's spiritual and aesthetic values.

This porcelain figure of a lion, originating from the Tang dynasty in China and dating from 618-906 CE, exemplifies the refined craftsmanship of the era. It is crafted from buff porcelain and adorned with a cream and green splashed glaze, giving it a distinctive and vibrant appearance. The lion, a common subject in Tang dynasty art, symbolizes power and protection, reflecting the cultural significance of such figures in Chinese tradition. This artifact was found in China, contributing to our understanding of Tang dynasty artistry and its legacy in ceramic production.

This Tang dynasty figure, made between 618-906 CE, represents a lady crafted from glazed straw earthenware, reflecting the period's artistic aesthetics and craftsmanship. The use of glazed earthenware was prevalent in the Tang dynasty for both decorative and functional objects, showcasing the era's advancements in ceramic technology. This scarab was excavated at Enkomi, providing valuable insight into the cross-cultural exchanges between Egypt and surrounding regions during this era.

description: This disc-shaped scaraboid, originating from the 26th Dynasty of Ancient Egypt and dated between 600-570 BC, is a captivating artifact crafted from glazed composition. It features a slightly domed, plain back with nearly straight sides and is pierced through its diameter. The underside displays a crudely incised engraving of a falcon holding a flail to the left, an oval containing three debased hieroglyphic signs to the right, and a flattened neb-basket symbol beneath. Some of the original buff-yellow glaze, pitted with small porosities, remains as a skin over its surface, with a slightly yellower and smoother core revealed beneath. The inscription is in hieroglyphic form and cautiously transliterated as "wAH-[jb]-ra," potentially translating to "Wahibre (Constant is the Heart of Re)." This could correspond to the nswt-bjt name of either Psamtek I or the title of Apries, reflecting possible links to these significant figures. The artifact was excavated in Naukratis, a site known for its rich connection to cross-cultural exchange in antiquity.

Crafted from a green-glazed composition, the figure represents Osorkon, adorned with a black curled page-boy wig and a distinctively modelled face. The shabti wears a garment with a deep v-neck and a pleated triangular apron, while one arm clasps a whip's handle across the chest, and the other drapes along its side. The lower section of the figure is missing below the knee, adding a sense of mystery to its incomplete form. Notably, the back features a central column of black-painted hieroglyphs that highlight Osorkon's prestigious title as High Priest of Ptah, inscribing both identity and status into the artifact. Discovered, or likely found, in Saqqara, an ancient necropolis serving Memphis, this shabti reflects the funerary traditions of embedding the deceased with figures believed to act as servants in the afterlife.

Transliteration suggests the inscription represents a shortened version of the royal name Psamtek, likely referring to Psamtek II, and is associated with a solar disk sign, highlighting its connection to the ancient Egyptian solar cult. This artifact was excavated at the Scarab Factory, adding to our understanding of the production techniques and cultural significance of scaraboids in Ancient Egypt.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: underside Inscription language: Egyptian Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription transliteration: jmn-ra Inscription translation: Amun-Ra
description: This Ancient Egyptian scaraboid, dating from approximately 600-570 BC, originates from the 26th Dynasty and was discovered at the renowned Scarab Factory. It is a mould-made, disc-shaped artifact crafted from a glazed composition, featuring a slightly domed and plain back with sides likely straight, although the side view is unknown. Notably, the underside is adorned with a stamped hieroglyphic inscription naming Amun-Ra, the revered deity, encircled by a groove near the edge. The piece is pierced through its diameter, and despite being described as unbaked and unglazed in certain records, faint traces of a greenish glaze suggest otherwise. The scaraboid's yellowish-beige paste forms a striking backdrop, despite one side being broken. This artifact provides insight into the religious and cultural symbolism prevalent in Ancient Egypt during this period.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: Front Inscription language: Egyptian Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription transliteration: jmn-ra wp rnpt nfr [...] Inscription translation: May Amun-Ra inaugurate a perfect year [...] Inscription note: Traditional wishes found on New Year's flasks.
description: This artifact is a glazed composition New Year's flask from the Late Period, specifically the 26th Dynasty of Ancient Egypt, dating to approximately the 6th century BC. The flask, though partially preserved, displays intricate geometric designs such as tear drops and rectangles arranged in a broad collar of concentric registers on its upper body. A central vertical band features a hieroglyphic inscription, which is framed by vertical bands decorated with a scale pattern. The inscription, rendered in Egyptian hieroglyphics, translates to a traditional blessing: "May Amun-Ra inaugurate a perfect year." Crafted using a mould-made technique from a now glaze-lost greenish-yellow fine paste, this object reflects the cultural significance of Amun-Ra in New Year rituals. The flask was excavated at Naukratis, one of the key Greek trading hubs in Egypt, emphasizing its role in cultural exchanges of the period.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: underside Inscription language: Egyptian Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription transliteration: jmn-ra Inscription translation: Amun-Ra Inscription note: Note the three vertical strokes, usually indicative of plural, but used here as a  filler.
description: This intricately crafted scarab from the 26th Dynasty of Ancient Egypt, dated between 600-570 BC, exemplifies the sophistication of the period's artistry. Mould-made from glazed composition, the scarab's design features skewed markings across the back, including a miniature clypeus, a single line denoting the prothorax, and elytra marked by a double suture with distinct humeral callosities depicted as winglets. The back is notably flattened, while the legs are simply represented. The underside bears a vertically arranged hieroglyphic inscription within a groove near the edge, naming the deity Amun-Ra, and includes three redundant vertical strokes, which are typically a plural marker but here serve as decorative fillers. The glaze, well-preserved in a pale yellow hue, contrasts with the core's dirty yellow tone. This artifact, pierced longitudinally, was discovered at the 'Scarab Factory' excavation site, encapsulating the religious and cultural significance of the scarab in ancient Egyptian society as a symbol of transformation and protection.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: leg section Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription translation: Titles/epithets include : Lady of the Two Lands; Divine Adoratrix
description: This artifact is a green-blue glazed composition shabti from the Third Intermediate Period of Ancient Egypt, specifically dated between 945 and 720 BC. The figurine is detailed with a lappet-wig and fillet, a modeled face with traced eyes, and indistinct hands holding two hoes, symbolizing its purpose as a funerary servant. Hieroglyphic inscriptions are present on the leg section, bestowing titles such as "Lady of the Two Lands" and "Divine Adoratrix" upon Qedmerut, to whom the shabti is dedicated. A seed-basket is depicted on the back, reinforcing its function in assisting with agricultural tasks in the afterlife. This shabti was discovered in Egypt, exemplifying the religious and cultural practices of the time associated with burial and the afterlife.

The underside is particularly fascinating, bearing a cryptographic inscription rendered in hieroglyphs featuring a falcon, men-draughtboard sign, and sun-disc, likely stamped around a groove near the edge. Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: underside Inscription language: Egyptian Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription transliteration: Pa-imen Inscription translation: The gift of Amun
description: This artifact is a mould-made scarab from the 26th Dynasty of Ancient Egypt, dating to approximately 600-570 BC. Crafted from a glazed composition, this scarab is notably worn, with the back and legs eroded from its sides. Despite its condition, traces of its original yellow glaze persist on the light yellow, cream paste material. It features a deeply incised hieroglyphic inscription on its underside, vertically arranged and pierced lengthwise, which translates to "The gift of Amun," indicating its religious significance and connection to the deity Amun. This scarab, a symbol of regeneration and protection in Egyptian culture, was excavated from Naukratis, a significant site for understanding Egyptian and Greek cultural interactions.

description: This captivating faience scarab from the Third Intermediate Period, dating circa 700 BCE, exemplifies the artistry of Ancient Egypt. Crafted from glazed composition material, the scarab is intricately engraved with a hieroglyphic inscription that reads either "Sebekhetep" or "offered to Sebek." The reverse side is distinguished by a detailed depiction of an African's head, a unique feature that adds to its cultural richness. Sobekhotep or the deity Sobek may be referenced in the inscription, linking the object to prominent figures or divine reverence within Egyptian mythology. This artifact was excavated from the Acropolis at Kamiros, indicating its journey from the heart of Egypt to the diverse lands of the Mediterranean.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription note: Inlaid.
description: This intricately designed pectoral, dating circa 1250 BC from the 19th Dynasty of Ancient Egypt, is crafted from glazed composition in shades of yellow, purple, blue, and white. Its form replicates a pylon, the monumental gateway of an Egyptian temple, complete with a cavetto cornice that mimics the stylized curved reed heads. Each face is adorned with a block decoration pattern. The upper surface features a reclining jackal named Anubis, the god of embalming, on a pylon-shaped plinth, accompanied by hieroglyphic inscriptions inlaid with precision. The underside displays a 'djed' pillar, symbolizing the backbone of Osiris, the god of the dead, flanked by the Girdle of Isis or 'tit' amulet, both serving as funerary amulets. Pierced holes in the cornice suggest the piece was affixed to a mummy's chest bandages, underscoring its funerary significance. This artifact, found in Egypt, exemplifies the religious and artistic practices of the period, highlighting the profound symbolism integral to Ancient Egyptian culture.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: underside Inscription language: Egyptian Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription transliteration: jmn rʿ (?) Inscription translation: Amun-Ra Inscription note: The Maat feather sign is used instead of a yod sign.
description: This exquisite Ancient Egyptian scarab, dating from approximately 600 to 570 BC, hails from the 26th Dynasty and is crafted from a glazed composition. Likely mould-made, the scarab's underside is adorned with a hieroglyphic inscription, proclaiming the revered name of the god Amun-Ra. The surface, as noted in Gardner's drawing, shows signs of erosion, yet the inscription remains partially discernible. The hieroglyphic script notably uses the Maat feather sign in place of a yod sign, a unique characteristic in its depiction of the deity. This artifact was uncovered at Naukratis, an important archeological site in Egypt, providing valuable insights into the religious practices and artistic traditions of the period.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription position: base Inscription script: hieroglyphic Inscription transliteration: hmt-nswt-ty Inscription translation: Queen Tiy
description: This faience scarab, dating from 1390-1352 BCE, originates from the Egyptian 18th Dynasty, a period marked by significant cultural and artistic achievements. Crafted from glazed composition, this artifact is engraved with intricate details depicting elytra, head, and legs, alongside a longitudinal piercing. The base of the scarab bears a hieroglyphic inscription that translates to "Queen Tiy," referencing the esteemed wife of Pharaoh Amenhotep III. While the scarab is noted to be poorly preserved, it still offers a glimpse into the artistry and iconography associated with royal figures of ancient Egypt. This piece was excavated at Enkomi, adding a layer of historical significance and providing insights into the distribution and influence of Egyptian culture beyond its borders.

The scarab's back is simply modeled with delineations of the clypeus, head, prothorax, and elytra marked by single lines, while the side view remains unknown. Unique features include the underside, which is stamped rather than incised, showcasing a hieroglyphic representation of a walking goose or duck, emphasized by a sun-disc above and a potential neb-basket sign to the right. Despite traces of a light blue glaze, it was possibly intended as unbaked and unglazed, crafted in a bluish-white paste that shows some surface wear. The hieroglyphic inscription, though challenging to translate, alludes to divine associations, potentially naming Amun-Ra, and symbolically refers to "The son of Ra is the lord" or "Amun-Ra is the lord," with the neb-basket sign possibly serving as ornamental filler. The scarab was excavated at the Scarab Factory, underscoring its cultural significance in the context of Egyptian religious and artistic traditions.

description: This scaraboid from the 26th Dynasty of Ancient Egypt, produced circa 600-570 BC, is a fascinating artifact crafted from glazed composition. The artifact is uniquely designed with the back in the form of a Black African head, featuring hair represented by squares and crudely cut facial features. Its underside is inscribed with incised hieroglyphs arranged horizontally, depicting symbols such as the Maat feather, a walking goose or duck, and a sun-disc. The object is created in black paste, with glaze absent due to either loss or lack of application, resulting in a quite eroded surface. The inscription, rendered in Egyptian hieroglyphs, intriguingly references deities such as Shu, son of Ra, and Amun-Ra, as well as Amun, highlighting its possible symbolic significance. This object was excavated in Naukratis, offering insights into the mélange of cultural influences in Ancient Egypt and the interplay of art and religion within the society.

description: This exquisite shabti figure, originating from ancient Egypt during the Third Intermediate Period (945-720 BC), is crafted from a faded green glazed composition. It features intricate black detailing that has since turned purple. The artifact depicts Tentast, as identified by the hieroglyphic inscription on the front. The figure is adorned with a lappet-wig secured by a fillet, a modelled face, and crossed arms that hold two hoes, symbolizing its function in accompanying the deceased into the afterlife to perform agricultural labor. A seed-basket is prominently displayed on the back, further reinforcing its purpose. This artifact was found in Egypt, a testament to the rich funerary traditions and artistic prowess of the period.
