description: This ancient Egyptian artifact is a small mould-made scarab, crafted between 600 BC and 570 BC during the 26th Dynasty. Fashioned from Egyptian blue paste of fine texture, the scarab is notably bright in color, despite its eroded condition. While the back of the piece is broken, the sides reveal simply modeled legs with an undercut triangle. The underside features an incised depiction of a winged seated griffin facing right, flanked by what appears to be a Maat feather symbol. Adjacent is a partially engraved cartouche containing three debased hieroglyphic signs, possibly representing the Horus name of Psamtek I or the nomen of Apries. A vertical line separates the inscription from the griffin. The artifact is longitudinally pierced, indicating it may have been used as an amulet or ornament. This scarab was possibly excavated from Naukratis, a significant trade hub in Egypt, offering insights into the cultural and symbolic exchanges of the time.

This quiver fitting, originating from the Middle Kofun period in Japan and dated circa 450-500 CE, exemplifies the sophisticated craftsmanship of the era through its use of gilt bronze. The fitting, a component of a quiver, was skillfully gilded, showcasing the amalgamation of bronze and gold, which underscores the aesthetic and functional priorities of this historical period. It was discovered at the Shibayama dolmen, a significant archaeological findspot that offers insights into the burial practices and martial culture of ancient Japan. This artifact reflects the intricate metallurgical techniques and the cultural significance tied to the martial elite of the Kofun period.

description: These ten stoneware sherds, originating from the Kofun Period and dating between 250-600 CE, were discovered at the Asakura Dolmen in Japan. The fragments feature the distinctive tataki technique, characterized by matted paddle and anvil marks, suggesting their utilitarian use in ancient ceramic practices. The largest sherd bears a handwritten English inscription: "Iyo, Asakusa No. 7 Dolmen (outside) 8/10/88," possibly serving as a later cataloging mark. This collection of sherds provides valuable insight into the craftsmanship and material culture of early Japanese society, particularly the funerary practices associated with the Kofun Period.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: 10cho N of Okamachi (Settsu)
description: This Late Kofun period Futatsuki dish with a lid, dating to 650 CE, exemplifies the high-fired stoneware craftsmanship prevalent in ancient Japan. The dish features a round base with a slightly inclining short rim, designed to accommodate the fitted lid. The lid itself is characterized by its slightly flattened top and a rim formed between the top and its sides, demonstrating the functional elegance of the era's utilitarian ceramics. An inscription in English, denoting "10cho N of Okamachi (Settsu)," provides locational context, suggesting its origins or use in the region. This artifact was found in Okamachi, further anchoring its historical and cultural significance within the Japanese landscape of the time.

This artifact is a fragmentary Takatsuki, representing the pedestal of a pedestal bowl from the Kofun Period, crafted between 250-600 CE. Made of high-fired stoneware, it features distinctively three perforations, a characteristic of pierced technique used during its creation. As part of Japanese cultural heritage, this piece exemplifies the ceramic craftsmanship of the Kofun Period. The fragment was discovered in Ibaraki-ken, Japan, contributing to the understanding of ancient Japanese ceremonial and utilitarian vessels.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: Akasaka, dolmen near
description: This Late Kofun period sagebe, a hanging jar dating from 700-750 CE, exemplifies the high-fired stoneware craftsmanship of Japan. The jar features a circular body with one side flattened and the other spherical, lending a distinctive and intriguing form. It is adorned with a natural ash glaze, indicative of traditional Japanese glazing techniques. The short neck flares into a wide mouth, and the addition of round knobs on the shoulder serves as stylized jug handles. An inscription in English mentions "Akasaka, dolmen near," providing context to its provenance or possible site of acquisition. Discovered near Akasaka-cho, this artifact offers a glimpse into the utilitarian and artistic expressions of Late Kofun Japan, reflecting the era's sophisticated ceramic traditions.

This Middle Kofun quiver fitting, dating from circa 450-500 CE, is an exquisite example of early Japanese craftsmanship. Constructed from bronze and skillfully gilded, the fitting exhibits the era's intricate metalwork techniques. Associated with the equestrian culture prominent during the Kofun period, this artifact exemplifies the artistic emphasis on elaborate and decorative armor and weapon accessories. Its provenance traces back to Shibayama dolmen, enriching our understanding of burial customs and the symbolic significance of martial equipment within Kofun society.

description: This triangular sherd from a high-fired stoneware vessel dates back to the Kofun Period, approximately between 250-600 CE. It is characterized by the distinctive tataki technique, which imparts a matted paddle mark texture on its surface, a hallmark of Japanese craftsmanship of the era. An inscription is etched on the underside, in English, stating "Miyohoji mura. Below mound near the dolmen 3/4/84," providing insight into its original context and location. Discovered at Myohoji in Japan, this artifact is a significant fragment reflecting the ceramic practices and material culture of ancient Japan.

This Yokobe, a barrel-shaped jar from the Kofun Period, dates back to between 250-552 CE and is a representative artifact of the Japanese cultural heritage. Crafted from high-fired stoneware, the jar features a wide mouth and short neck, characteristic of its functional design. Its exterior showcases tataki matted paddle marks, a technique indicative of its time, while the interior bears anvil marks, suggesting the artisans' skilled craftsmanship. Kiln wasters adhering to the sides provide insight into its production process and the kiln settings of the period. This artifact was found in or acquired from the historic region of Izumi, offering a glimpse into the material culture of ancient Japan.

This collection of five roof-tile fragments, crafted in green glazed stoneware, hails from the illustrious Daigokuden and dates back to 794-795 CE, during Japan's Heian Period. As architectural remnants, these tiles provide a tangible link to the opulent structures of their time, reflecting the sophisticated tile production techniques employed for imperial buildings. Glazed to a rich green hue, these fragments contribute valuable insights into the aesthetic and functional considerations of early Japanese architecture. Unearthed at Nijo-jo, they offer a glimpse into the material culture and architectural advancements of Japan's capital cities in the late 8th century.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription quoted: Kawachi
description: This Middle Kofun period jar, dated between 400-450 CE, exemplifies Japanese ceramic artistry through its high-fired stoneware composition and natural ash glaze finish. Its globular body features a rounded base, with the neck elegantly spreading towards the mouth. The jar is adorned with kakime bands—wavy patterns skillfully incised with an eight-pointed comb, accentuating the shoulders and repeating between two raised ridges along the neck. An inscription referencing "Kawachi" suggests historical significance, possibly linked to its excavation site in Kawachi, a once-prominent kuni (historic province) of Japan. This artifact reflects the sophisticated craftsmanship and aesthetic sensibilities of the Kofun period, providing insight into the cultural practices of the time.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: Mino. near Kiyomizu 3 ri from Akasaka
description: This Late Kofun period sagebe, a hanging jar crafted between 550-599 CE, epitomizes the exquisite artistry of early Japanese stoneware. Made from high-fired stoneware with a natural ash glaze, the jar features a unique form with a circular body, comprising one flat and one spherical side. Its short neck gracefully expands towards the mouth, flanked by two round handles on the shoulders. The jar is meticulously decorated with fine incised spiral lines and two bands of radiating ornament, showcasing the skilled incising techniques of the time. An English inscription notes the proximity to "Mino, near Kiyomizu 3 ri from Akasaka," linking it to the historical rich region of Japan. This remarkable artifact was found at Akasaka-cho, near the Kiyomizu dolmens, providing a tangible connection to the Late Kofun period and offering valuable insights into the ceramic practices and cultural dimensions of ancient Japan.

This exquisite jar from the Late Kofun period, crafted between 650-700 CE, epitomizes the high-fired stoneware artistry of ancient Japan. Featuring a globular body with a rounded base and a short neck that elegantly flares towards the mouth, the jar is accented by circular handles affixed to each shoulder. The exterior showcases distinctive tataki matted paddle marks, a testament to the period's ceramic techniques, while the interior bears the hallmark round anvil marks. Shellfish fragments adhere to its surface, hinting at its historical and geographical journey. This artifact was discovered in the Yasui rock tomb in Japan, providing valuable insight into the burial practices and material culture of the era.

This quiver fitting, dating approximately from 450-500 CE, originates from the Middle Kofun period in Japan. The artifact is crafted from bronze and features a gilded surface, showcasing the sophisticated metalworking techniques of the era. Its discovery in the Shibayama dolmen highlights its cultural significance, as quiver fittings were often associated with the burial practices and status of individuals during the Kofun period. This piece serves as a testament to the artistry and ceremonial customs of ancient Japanese society.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription language: English Inscription quoted: Mino near Kiyomizu 3 ri from Akasaka
description: This Late Kofun period pedestal long-necked jar, dating to around 600 CE, is a striking example of Japanese stoneware craftsmanship. Constructed from high-fired stoneware, it features a natural ash glaze that imparts a durable, aesthetically pleasing surface. The jar's globular body is designed with a flattened shoulder, resting on a pedestal which flares towards the foot, and it possesses a neck that also expands towards the mouth. Artistic embellishments include incised grooves that accentuate the pedestal, body, and neck, with the pedestal itself exhibiting three long vertical perforations, adding to its visual intrigue. An English inscription references "Mino near Kiyomizu 3 ri from Akasaka." This artifact was discovered near Akasaka-cho, situating it geographically within Japan and providing insight into the region's ceramic traditions during this era.

Inscription: Inscription type: inscription Inscription quoted: Nose
description: This Late Kofun period sagebe, crafted around 600 CE in Japan, is a sophisticated hanging jar made of high-fired stoneware, distinguished by its natural ash glaze. It features a circular body with one side flattened and the opposite side spherical, a design that exemplifies the era's aesthetic sensitivity. The jar boasts a short neck that elegantly expands toward the mouth, complemented by small hook-shaped handles attached to its shoulders. Both sides of the jar are adorned with spiraling incised lines, adding to its visual intrigue. An inscription quoted as "Nose" further enhances its historical significance, connecting it to the Settsu region in the historic Kuni Nose district, where it was found. This artifact is a testament to the technical and artistic prowess of potters during the Late Kofun period in Japan.

This collection of five vessel sherds originates from the Kofun Period of Japan, dating between 250-600 CE. Crafted from high-fired stoneware, these fragments display remnants of natural ash glaze and visible tataki paddle and anvil marks, reflecting traditional Japanese ceramic techniques. Handwritten English inscriptions on labels accompany the pieces, detailing their provenance with references to a partially, and at times completely, destroyed mound at Domyoji, the location where they were discovered. These sherds provide a tangible connection to the Kofun era’s cultural practices and ceramic craftsmanship, underscoring the sophisticated aesthetics and functional artistry prevalent during this period in Japan.

This carved stone equine figure, originating from Japan's Kofun Period, dates back to approximately 250-600 CE. The sculpture, representing a horse or ass, is intricately carved, reflecting the skill and artistry associated with this era in Japanese history. The Kofun Period is marked by its distinctive burial mounds and funerary art, of which this figure is a fine example. Discovered in the historic region of Yamato, this artifact highlights the cultural and symbolic significance of equines in Japanese society during this time, often associated with status and spiritual beliefs.

Constructed from green glazed stoneware, the sherd exhibits unique surface textures, including tataki matted paddle marks and carved anvil marks on the underside. It bears an English inscription on a label, noting its proximity to Misao-yama near Okayama, with a reference to dolmen number 13, suggestive of its archaeological context. This piece was discovered at the Misaoyama Dolmen, linking it to the rich funerary traditions of the Kofun Period. Such artifacts provide valuable insight into the material culture and techniques, such as glazing and decoration, employed during this prehistoric era in Japan.

Below mound near the dolmen," providing contextual provenance of its discovery at Myohoji, Japan. This artifact, found near a dolmen, underlines the historical and cultural practices of burial and pottery production during this significant era of early Japanese society.

This assemblage of 14 sherds, dating from 550-620 CE, originates from the Late Kofun period in Japan. Crafted from high-fired stoneware, each piece exhibits the distinctive tataki technique, characterized by impressions made using a carved anvil on the interior and a matted paddle on the exterior. These artifacts, emblematic of the technological and artistic advancements of the era, were discovered or acquired in Ryoseki, although the exact findspot remains uncertain. The sherds offer valuable insights into the ceramic practices and cultural expressions of Japan during the Late Kofun period.

description: This late Kofun period stoneware artifact, produced between 750-800 CE, is a lid of a Takatsuki, or pedestal bowl, showcasing the refined craftsmanship of ancient Japan. Fashioned from dark grey high-fired stoneware, the lid features a prominent knob and intricate decorative incisions, including two concentric grooves encircling it, with a band of oblique strokes artfully nestled between them. An inscription, reading "Hattorigawa Kawachi, 13/2/86," is present, potentially indicating the site of discovery or other contextual details. Unearthed at Hattorigawa in Japan, this relic provides valuable insight into the artisanal techniques and cultural expressions of the Late Kofun period, enriching our understanding of Japan's historical and artistic heritage.

This exquisite ornamental harness pendant from the Kofun Period, dating between 250-600 CE, exemplifies the metallurgical artistry of ancient Japan. Crafted from a combination of gilt bronze, iron, and silver, the pendant features a distinctive design where an oval is seamlessly integrated with an attached rhombus. Such pendants were traditionally affixed to the harnesses of horses, serving both functional and decorative purposes. The gilded finish enhances its luxurious appearance, reflecting the cultural emphasis on elaborate equestrian adornments during this era.
